notes:
Task and constraints: Identify which receptor receives a light ray reflected inside a square room with side length p and vertical offset q.
Idea: Use the least common multiple of p and q to find the number of horizontal and vertical traversals until the ray reaches a corner.
Technique and why it applies: L/q counts vertical segments and L/p counts horizontal segments. Their parity determines which wall corner is reached.
Invariant: L is the smallest shared travel length that aligns both dimensions at a corner.
Edge cases: lcm is used without being imported or defined in the snippet. The method assumes p and q are positive and q is within the room height.
Complexity: Computing the LCM depends on the implementation of lcm; with a Euclidean GCD it is O(log min(p,q)) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine the receptor hit by a ray reflected in a square room of side p with offset q.
Idea: Compute the LCM of p and q and inspect the parity of the horizontal and vertical reflection counts.
Technique and why it applies: lcm/p counts room widths traversed and lcm/q counts room heights. Their odd/even combination identifies receptor 0, 1, or 2.
Invariant: lcm is the smallest common travel distance reaching a corner.
Edge cases: The custom gcd loop handles positive integers; p and q must be nonzero for division. The output cases are exhaustive for the problem's positive inputs.
Complexity: Euclidean GCD computes the LCM in O(log min(p,q)) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Find the receptor reached by a ray reflected inside a square room.
Idea: Compare the lowest set-bit values of p and q to determine their powers-of-two parity relationship.
Technique and why it applies: The low bit p & -p captures the largest power of two dividing p; comparing these values identifies the same odd/even reflection cases as reducing p and q by common factors of two.
Invariant: The comparison of low-bit factors encodes the parity pattern of the room-width and room-height counts.
Edge cases: The formula assumes p and q are positive integers, as specified. The nested conditional maps equal low bits to receptor 1, p's factor greater to 2, and lower to 0.
Complexity: Bit operations and comparisons take O(1) time and O(1) space for bounded integer arithmetic.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two strings can become equal by swapping exactly two characters in one string.
Idea: Compare positions where s and goal differ; either there must be exactly two cross-matching differences or identical strings with a repeated character.
Technique and why it applies: Swapping the two mismatched characters fixes both positions. If there are no mismatches, a repeated character permits a swap that leaves the string unchanged.
Invariant: diffCharactersInS and diffCharactersInGoal store the characters at each differing position.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths immediately fail. Counter is imported but only used for identical strings; strings with zero differences and all unique characters correctly return False.
Complexity: The scan and frequency count take O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check whether A and B are buddy strings, meaning one swap in A can make it equal to B.
Idea: Collect mismatched character pairs and accept either two reversed pairs or identical strings with duplicate characters.
Technique and why it applies: Exactly two differences must cross-match after a swap. With no differences, swapping equal characters preserves A, possible only if A has a duplicate.
Invariant: diff contains at most two pairs of characters from corresponding positions.
Edge cases: Different lengths fail. The early return on more than two differences avoids unnecessary scanning; importing itertools is unnecessary.
Complexity: One pass and set construction take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether every customer can receive correct change when lemonade costs five dollars.
Idea: Track counts of five- and ten-dollar bills and use larger bills only when sufficient smaller change is available.
Technique and why it applies: A ten-dollar bill requires one five-dollar bill; a twenty-dollar bill is paid back preferentially with one ten and one five, or three fives.
Invariant: five and ten represent the cash currently available for making change.
Edge cases: Bills are expected to be 5, 10, or 20. The conditions reject any twenty-dollar payment that cannot be changed with the available bills.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Check whether the lemonade stand can give correct change to every customer.
Idea: Maintain counts of five- and ten-dollar bills and process each payment greedily.
Technique and why it applies: Five-dollar bills are the only change for a ten-dollar payment. For twenty, using a ten plus a five preserves more five-dollar bills than using three fives when possible.
Invariant: five and ten are the bills available after processing the customer prefix.
Edge cases: The code treats any bill other than 5 or 10 as a 20-dollar bill, relying on the input domain. It returns False immediately when change cannot be made.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the lemonade stand can make exact change for each customer.
Idea: Track counts of denominations and greedily assemble each customer's change from largest denominations downward.
Technique and why it applies: For each bill, the code increments its count, computes change relative to five dollars, then consumes available 20s, 10s, and 5s to cover it.
Invariant: counts stores the inventory after receiving the current bill and before returning change.
Edge cases: This approach is incorrect for the standard problem: it adds the incoming bill to counts and may use that same bill as change, and the greedy denomination loop may not preserve the needed five-dollar bills. The unused collections import does not affect the logic.
Complexity: Each payment checks three denominations, giving O(n) time and O(1) denomination space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the binary score of a matrix by flipping any rows and columns.
Idea: Account for making the first column all ones, then independently choose the better orientation for each remaining column.
Technique and why it applies: Flipping a row to make its first bit one is equivalent to XORing every cell with that row's first bit. Each column contributes the larger of its one-count and zero-count times its binary positional weight.
Invariant: A[r][c] XOR A[r][0] represents the bit in column c after the row has been oriented to start with one.
Edge cases: The method assumes a nonempty rectangular matrix. It does not mutate A.
Complexity: Counting all cells takes O(RC) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest nonempty subarray whose sum is at least K, even when nums contains negative values.
Idea: Build prefix sums and maintain their indices in a monotonic increasing deque.
Technique and why it applies: If the current prefix minus the oldest prefix is at least K, a qualifying subarray is found and the start index is removed to seek a shorter one. Larger tail prefixes are removed because a later smaller prefix dominates them.
Invariant: Prefix sums at indices in monoq are strictly increasing, and candidate starts remain in index order.
Edge cases: deque is used without being imported. The initial prefix sum zero allows subarrays beginning at index zero; no solution returns -1.
Complexity: Each prefix index enters and leaves the deque at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the minimum length of a nonempty subarray with sum at least K.
Idea: Compute prefix sums and use a monotonic deque to find shortest valid prefix differences.
Technique and why it applies: Removing tail indices with prefix sums no smaller than the current sum preserves only useful starts. Popping front indices that satisfy K updates the shortest result.
Invariant: accumulated_sum stores prefix totals, and mono_increasing_q holds indices with increasing prefix values.
Edge cases: Negative numbers are supported, so ordinary sliding windows would not be valid. Empty input returns -1 because no qualifying prefix pair is found.
Complexity: Each index is pushed and popped once, giving O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of steps to collect all keys in a grid while unlocking doors.
Idea: Run BFS over position and the set of keys currently held.
Technique and why it applies: Each move costs one step; keys extend the key string and locked doors are entered only when their matching lowercase key is present. Visited states prevent repeated exploration.
Invariant: q stores states reachable in the current step count, and visited records processed (row,column,keys) triples.
Edge cases: deque is used without an import in the snippet. Keys are stored as a string, so collection order can differ and cause duplicate logical states; the code does not normalize the key order. keyCt counts key cells, assuming one of each key.
Complexity: The state space is O(RC·2^K) in principle, but string-based key tracking can create extra duplicate states; time and space are exponential in the number of keys.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest path that collects every key in a grid with locked doors and walls.
Idea: Precompute shortest distances between the start, keys, and doors, then run Dijkstra over location and a key bitmask.
Technique and why it applies: Grid BFS computes distances to the next special location while treating walls as blocked. Dijkstra then combines those distances, only allowing a door destination if its key bit is set.
Invariant: best[place][state] stores the least total distance to a special location with the given collected-key mask.
Edge cases: The condition source != grid[r][c] != '.' is a chained comparison, not a simple inequality test; it may stop at special cells as intended but should be read carefully. The target mask assumes keys are labeled consecutively from a.
Complexity: Precomputation runs BFS from each special cell, about O(KRC), then Dijkstra explores up to O(K·2^K) states and transitions.

Task and constraints: Find the smallest prime palindrome greater than or equal to N.
Idea: Generate odd-length palindromes by mirroring the prefix, then test candidates for primality.
Technique and why it applies: Every even-length palindrome greater than 11 is divisible by 11, so after the special case the search can focus on odd-length palindromes. Trial division tests each candidate.
Invariant: Each generated j is a palindrome formed from prefix i and its reversed prefix without the final digit.
Edge cases: N between 8 and 11 returns 11. The loop has a fixed prefix upper bound of 10^5 and has no explicit fallback return if no candidate is found within that bound.
Complexity: For each generated candidate, primality testing takes O(sqrt(j)) time; the overall search is bounded by the prefix range and candidate primality cost.

Task and constraints: Transpose a rectangular matrix, turning rows into columns.
Idea: Allocate a result with reversed dimensions and assign each source cell to result[c][r].
Technique and why it applies: Transposition swaps row and column indices, so an R-by-C matrix becomes C-by-R.
Invariant: result[c][r] equals A[r][c] for every processed cell.
Edge cases: The code assumes A has at least one row because it reads A[0]. Empty rows produce an empty result with zero rows or columns according to dimensions.
Complexity: Each cell is copied once, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) output space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest distance between consecutive set bits in the binary representation of n.
Idea: Scan the binary string after its leading one and track the previous set-bit position.
Technique and why it applies: Each new one completes a candidate gap from the prior one; res stores the maximum distance seen.
Invariant: prev is the position of the most recent one in the sliced binary representation, adjusted relative to that slice.
Edge cases: If n has fewer than two set bits, the result remains zero. The indexing starts from bin(n)[3:], omitting the leading bit and first following position; this offset scheme is subtle and should be checked on small values.
Complexity: Converting to binary and scanning takes O(log n) time and O(log n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum gap between adjacent ones in the binary representation of N.
Idea: Inspect each bit position and remember the previous position containing a one.
Technique and why it applies: The distance between consecutive set-bit indices is the binary gap; the maximum of those distances is the answer.
Invariant: last is the most recently observed set-bit position, and result is the largest gap found so far.
Edge cases: Numbers with fewer than two set bits return zero. The loop checks 32 bit positions, matching the problem's integer bound.
Complexity: A fixed 32 iterations gives O(1) time and O(1) space under the constraint.

Task and constraints: Permute nums1 so as many positions as possible have nums1[i] greater than nums2[i].
Idea: Sort nums1 and process nums2 from largest value to smallest, assigning the smallest winning value or sacrificing the smallest value.
Technique and why it applies: A max-heap orders indices by nums2 value. If the largest remaining nums1 value cannot beat the current nums2 maximum, the smallest nums1 value is sacrificed there; otherwise the largest is used to win.
Invariant: l and r bound the unused sorted nums1 values, and ans assigns each processed nums2 position once.
Edge cases: heapq is used without an import in the snippet. nums1 is sorted in place. Equal values do not count as a win because the comparison is strict.
Complexity: Heap operations take O(n log n) and sorting nums1 takes O(n log n), with O(n) extra space.

Task and constraints: Reorder nums1 to maximize the number of indices where nums1[i] exceeds nums2[i].
Idea: Sort both arrays, assign each value that can beat the smallest remaining target, and save losing values for the remaining positions.
Technique and why it applies: The sorted sweep pairs a winning value with the smallest target it can beat. Values that cannot beat that target are placed in others; the final pass assigns wins or sacrifices.
Invariant: candidates maps target values to winning nums1 values, while others stores values not assigned to a win.
Edge cases: candidates is keyed by value, so duplicate values in B share one list; the final pop operations may still distribute values but need careful scrutiny with duplicates and assignment order. The input lengths are assumed equal.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n), the sweep and output take O(n) expected time, and storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of refueling stops needed to reach target, given starting fuel and stations sorted by position.
Idea: Sweep stations in order and keep passed fuel amounts in a max-heap, refueling from the largest available amount whenever needed.
Technique and why it applies: When the next station is beyond current reach, the best available past station is chosen greedily because it provides the greatest increase in reach.
Invariant: heap stores negative fuel amounts for stations already passed, and F is the current reachable distance/fuel boundary as updated by refuels.
Edge cases: The method appends [t,0] directly to S, mutating the input. heapq is used without import. It assumes stations are sorted by position and each station is only considered once.
Complexity: Each station is pushed and popped at most once, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) heap space.
